title: Supervision 7 essay
description: How does an adult human respond to the ingestion of one litre of (a) fresh water; (b) isotonic saline; (c) seawater?
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 7. Write it here, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Planning. Plan your essay before you start writing, on paper if you like.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your work.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your work, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Saving. Your work is saved in this browser as you type, so you can stop and come back to it. It stays here until you submit it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your work and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Fresh water, saline and seawater
questions.text:
How does an adult human respond to the ingestion of one litre of (a) fresh water; (b) isotonic saline; (c) seawater?

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Support your argument with mechanisms, evidence and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers.

What the title asks. The responses, and the reasons for them, to three drinks of the same volume that add different things: water alone; water and salt in the proportions of the ECF; and more salt than water. Each part needs answering, but the essay is strongest when it uses the three to show how osmoregulation and volume regulation work, and which of them wins when they conflict.

  • The tools. About 40 L of body water (ICF 24–25 L, ECF 16 L, of which plasma is 3 L) at about 285–300 mOsm/kg; water crosses cell membranes freely, NaCl stays in the ECF. Osmoregulation: hypothalamic osmoreceptors (magnocellular neurones, with stretch-inactivated cation channels), ADH (aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct, and the urea permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct), and thirst (less sensitive: a rise of 2% or more). Volume regulation: the ECF volume depends on its Na+ content, because osmoregulation fixes its concentration; cardiopulmonary receptors and arterial baroreceptors, the renal sympathetic nerves, renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone, ANP, and physical factors (pressure natriuresis and the Starling forces in the peritubular capillaries).
  • Fresh water. It spreads through all the body water: the osmolality falls by about 2.4% (to about 293 mOsm/kg), the ECF gains 0.4 L and the cells 0.6 L, the plasma only about 75 mL, so there’s next to no volume signal. Less ADH (reflexes from the gut and liver begin to inhibit it even before absorption, a feed-forward), so the collecting ducts become impermeable and the dilute fluid from the loop of Henle passes into the urine: a water diuresis that starts within half an hour or so, and is mostly over within two or three hours, because ADH is released by nerves and cleared quickly. Thirst is suppressed.
  • Isotonic saline. It stays in the ECF: +1 L (6.25%), with no change in osmolality and none in the cells; the plasma gains about 0.2 L. Nothing for osmoregulation to correct, so only volume regulation responds: atrial stretch and more ANP; less renal sympathetic activity; less renin (the intrarenal baroreceptor, the macula densa and fewer β1 impulses), so less angiotensin II and aldosterone; pressure natriuresis; diluted plasma proteins, so a lower colloid osmotic pressure in the peritubular capillaries and less proximal reabsorption. Na+ excretion rises slowly: the excess takes up to a day or two to go.
  • Seawater (about 1000 mOsm/L, as in the lecture). At first it draws water into the gut, so the ECF shrinks (hypovolaemic thirst). Once it’s absorbed, the osmolality rises by about 6% (to about 317 mOsm/kg), water leaves the cells (about 1.3 L) and the ECF expands (by about 2.3 L). Osmotic stimuli win: maximal ADH and intense thirst, although the expanded volume would inhibit both (osmotic thirst overrides hypovolaemic thirst). The expanded ECF drives a natriuresis, but the urine can’t be concentrated beyond about 1200 mOsm/kg, and up to half of the medulla’s osmotic pressure is urea, so excreting the salt takes more water than was drunk: the net result is cellular dehydration.
  • The comparison. Speed: osmoregulation acts in minutes (neural release of ADH), volume regulation over hours to days (hormones and Na+ excretion). Priority: osmolality is defended within 1–2% at the expense of volume, which varies acutely by about −10% to +20%. And the sensors overlap: large falls in volume (over 10%) do release ADH and cause thirst, and angiotensin II causes drinking (Fitzsimons’s experiments in rats).

What makes an essay stand out. Numbers for each drink, from the compartments. A parallel structure that makes the comparisons easy. The time course of each response. The conflict in seawater resolved, with the reason. And a conclusion that says what the three cases show about how the two systems are organised.
